The Trial Chamber has decided to bring in the witness again, but he will only make his statement on the sole question that you have mentioned, and the Defence will have an opportunity to question him on that one point only. Bring in Mr. Djidic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Prosecutor has conveyed to us to a clarification that you wish to make, and the Trial Chamber will hear you on that one question that will be put to you by the Prosecutor, and we remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Prosecutor, will you please put the question that you raised yourself. After that, if the Defence has any cross-examination to make, it will do so. Mr. Prosecutor. MR. SEFKIJA DJIDIC (recalled)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President, your Honours. Mr. Djidic, concerning ammunition brought by a private entity, how did that ammunition get to you in Stari Vitez and in what manner was it brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When talking about ammunition and my statement about it, that I never received through the United Nations any ammunition, I wish to clear up a possible dilemma. Since Mr. Nobilo said that I had changed my testimony, I am not changing my testimony. I uphold what I said, that I never received through members of the United Nations any ammunition, and what General Alagic stated does not apply to the United Nations but it refers to a private organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you have any questions, any cross-examination of the witness on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Which organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a private organisation which does not belong to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What is its name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if I have to give you the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is important for us so that we can verify your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object at this point, your Honour, because of some danger expressed to members of that organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, the witness does not wish to answer your question. You will draw the conclusion you wish, which you consider to be opportune, emanating from the witness's failure to answer the question. In that case, the debate is closed on the question of ammunition. Mr. Djidic, we wish to thank you once again and ask the usher to take you out. Mr. Nobilo, have you more questions to put on this point? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just on this point only. Go ahead then, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did you get in touch with this private unnamed organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came to Stari Vitez on their own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In whose vehicles did they come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In their own vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In what way did that ammunition reach you, technically speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said, a small quantity of ammunition which came down the Lasva river, and another small quantity in a vehicle under the seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now you have given us a new piece of information. First it was just the river, now a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, I object to what Mr. Nobilo thinks is a new piece of information and request that Mr. Nobilo ask just questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I agree with you that Mr. Nobilo should not make any comments, but I do not agree with you with regard to the right of Mr. Nobilo to clear up this point. If he does not wish to give the name of the organisation, it is quite legitimate for the Defence to put certain questions to clarify the way in which that ammunition reached the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Along the Lasva river, what does that mean? What means of transport was used along the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A primitive device. It was a rubber tyre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How much ammunition did you get in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several hundred bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the civilian vehicle? How much ammunition did it bring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several hundred again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In addition to these two deliveries of several hundred, did you receive any further ammunition during the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Djidic, the Trial Chamber wishes to thank you. Please take the witness out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you have another witness, I assume?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecutor calls Sefik Pezer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before the witness enters, I should like to ask you, also on behalf of my colleagues, how much time have you planned for questioning this witness, and, on the other hand, I should like to remind you of the request made to Mr. Mark Harmon for a list which will be communicated to the judge of the number of witnesses that you wish to hear and the time with relative precision that you wish to devote to the examination-in-chief of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, with regard to your first question, I would anticipate the direct examination of Mr. Pezer to be approximately two hours, and the list that your Honour requested directly from Mr. Harmon, that is in my hand, in this red file right here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Please give us the list through the intermediary of the Registrar. Mr. Hayman, you have a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Before the next witness comes in, may I have a moment to confer with Mr. Nobilo and perhaps make a request to the court in light of the witness's refusal to answer a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. (Pause). Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I have spoken with my co-counsel concerning the issue of Mr. Djidic's refusal to answer the question concerning the source of these arms that reached him to assist the army in Stari Vitez during the siege. The Defence, we do not know of any rules that would permit a witness to refuse to answer questions. I note Rule 77(a), which states that a witness who refuses or fails contumaciously to answer a relevant question may be found in contempt, and then certain penalties are provided. In my system, it is also not uncommon for a witness who refuses to answer questions on cross-examination, for the witness's direct examination to be stricken, because the Defence and the accused has not been allowed to exercise its right of cross-examination where a witness declines to answer. Here I would suggest it is impermissible for the Prosecution to seek to prove that these arms did not come from one source, whether it is the Red Cross or the United Nations, and yet we the Defence were not able to explore the area because the witness simply refuses to say where in fact they did come from. I leave it to the court whether the direct examination should be stricken, or whether contempt proceedings should go forward against the witness or whether he should be given the opportunity to answer the question prior to contempt proceedings being brought, but we think there must be some remedy, or else what is to prevent other witnesses, if it causes embarrassment or discomfort, or perhaps might tend to incriminate a friend or relative -- we may have many witnesses who decline to answer difficult questions on cross-examination because they are difficult, and we do not believe that is adequate grounds for them to decline to answer such questions. If a question needs to be dealt with in closed session or subject to some type of protective order to the Defence, we have no objection to that, but we do object to allowing the witness not to answer the question. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber, Mr. Hayman, knows well Article 77 on contempt of the Tribunal, but it would like to say that this is a discretionary right of the Chamber, and it is a possibility, so that the Rule stipulated under 77(a) is limited by paragraph (b), that the Chamber may relieve the witness of the duty to answer, which it did so by saying that Mr. Nobilo can draw the necessary conclusions. Then there is another exception envisaged in Rule 90; the witness told you that he could endanger an organisation by mentioning it. To conclude, contempt of the Tribunal is an extremely difficult measure. I would not say it is rare, but it is relatively rare, and it is up to the discretion of the Chamber which does not find it necessary to raise the issue in this particular case with respect to this particular witness. I think therefore this matter of Mr. Djidic is closed. We can now proceed for about two hours to hear the next witness, which the usher will bring in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, can you hear me, please? Will you stand up if you can hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you tell the judges your name, your first and second name? What is your name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Sefik Pezer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Sefik Pezer, you can now read the solemn declaration which has been handed to you. SEFIK PEZER (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President, your Honours. Mr. Pezer, how old are you, sir, and do you have a family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 44; I have a wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What area of Bosnia do you live in now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I now live in a village within the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where did you grow up? Where were you born, where did you go to school and where did you spend most of your early years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 28th September 1953 in Klobje, the municipality of Zenica. From the age of 6 or 7 I lived in Vitez, Donje Dubravica, Novaci; that is the popular name for it. In 1976, when I got married, I got an apartment from my company, the company I worked for, and that is where I lived until the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you live in that location until 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, before the war broke out, what did you do for work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in the factory Slobodan Princip Seljo, from 1976 until the war, literally until the war broke out on 16th April 1993. That was my main occupation, and my wife was also employed. She worked for a private employer in the town itself, she worked in a catering establishment, Cevapcinica, and before the conflict in 1993, I rented a Cevapcinica from a man and that is where my wife started working and I helped her there too after all the work I did at my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were working in the SPS factory as well as helping your wife in the Cevapcinica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Using the exhibit to your left, the photograph on the easel, Mr. Pezer -- for the record, Mr. President, your Honours, we are referring to Prosecutor's exhibit 56 on the easel. Can you turn to that picture and with the assistance of the usher, could you use a pointer and show us where your Cevapi shop was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just find out where the north is on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is not very convenient for the witness, Mr. Prosecutor. It is not easy; he has to speak into the microphone, he has to look at the map. Let us try and facilitate his task. Bring the easel closer to him, perhaps. Mr. Registrar, perhaps you could help our witness a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The public gallery must be able to see and the Defence, of course, must be able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I approach the witness and be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You can help him, but you must not answer on his behalf, of course, just assist him physically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just have a look. This should be the place (indicates).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now the Defence cannot see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would it not be simpler, Mr. Prosecutor, that the witness simply tells us where the place he is looking for is? That would be simpler for understanding. Could the witness tell us where the establishment in question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Pezer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The railway station in Vitez. I have found it. Here it is (indicates). It is difficult to read this map really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, prior to you opening your Cevapi shop in that location, what was at that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you ask that more clearly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there another shop at your store prior to your opening up the Cevapi shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a Cevapi shop there before, and it was run by the man from whom I had rented the place. It worked for about a year and a half before it was blown up. Two bombs were thrown; one exploded, the other one did not, so I found it in a state of disrepair and then I agreed with the landlord that I would take the place over and continue working there because I thought simply that I could work there, because I had expected the Muslim and Croat people to reach neutral agreement and to have things function normally and that is the way it was. I worked in that same establishment for about a month but on 16th April, the war broke out, and everything came to a halt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, you said that the man who ran this shop before you and your wife, the store was blown up -- his store was blown up, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a bomb was thrown. I think it was January, February or March 1993. After that I changed the glass, repaired the ceramics, also there were some broken chairs, and then I repaired the place and restored it to its original appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that man a Muslim who was blown out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his name was Semsudin Subasic and he told me about it. After the incident he went to the police station in town. He complained but he did not receive any response and he simply closed the place down, and I wanted to make wooden shutters immediately, as soon as I took the place over, so that a new bomb could not be thrown again. There were three or four Croat shops in the area, so I thought, perhaps I can make it out there too, perhaps I can work alongside with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why did you think that you or your family was not going to be hurt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought because I was an ordinary citizen, I was not a soldier, I was not interested in politics simply, I was not interested in the war, I was not interested in the army, I was only interested in working, and, to tell you the truth, what I said, time and again, if there would be any fighting in Vitez it would only be the army and the HVO that would be fighting each other, the military units, but that the civilians would remain untouched. That is what I believed until the very last day. However my assessment was not correct. The worst possible thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, going back to the photograph, and you pointed to your Cevapi shop near the railway station in Dubravica, is the Dubravica school where the Vitezovi was, was that near to your Cevapi shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The school is about 200 metres away approximately. However, you can see it from the Cevapi shop because the school was on the hill and the Cevapi shop was underneath and there was a small forest in between but it was not very far away, about 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did members of the Vitezovi frequent your Cevapi shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they used to frequent it. They used to eat there, not all of them but quite a few of them. They used to eat there, some of them owed me money. They would not pay for the food they received, but that was not a meaningful amount. I did not pay much attention to it. I just thought, let it be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us move ahead, Mr. Pezer, to the day before the attack, 15th April 1993. Can you tell the judges, did you work that day, and if you did work, where did you work and where did you go after work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My usual working day was to work in the factory for eight hours and after 3 pm in the afternoon, I would help my wife. On that day, 15th April, I worked in the factory until 3 pm, then I came home, and then I went to the Cevapi shop to help my wife, to ask her whether she needed anything, whether I should go and buy something for her, do some shopping for her et cetera. When I came to the Cevapi shop it was full of people. I was sort of surprised because I was not used to that, I was not used to seeing such a full shop, and I asked my wife, "What is this?" She said the road to Zenica has been blocked and these people who are supposed to go to Zenica, to move further on, cannot go along that road, so they are taking a break, resting, eating, drinking et cetera, so we stayed there until about 5 pm. All the goods we had in the shop -- we had some reserves which could keep us going for about two or three days -- all of it was sold that day, so we had to close early that day because there was no need to wait any longer. As I was waiting for my wife to finish all her work, I spent some time in the shop itself. I spent some time outside because that was the main road to Zenica and Busovaca. I was standing in front of the shop and I saw unusual movements by HVO soldiers who were going by non-stop. They were going to the school; they were moving towards Zenica, towards Ahmici, Novaci, but I could not imagine that something like that could happen on 16th April. The only thing I found suspicious was that the members of the HVO on that very same day, that is to say after 3 pm when I was there, they also drove along taking some fuel in a vehicle, and they also had a three-barrel anti-artillery gun on a FAP vehicle, mounted on the vehicle. I saw them go to Novaci and go back several times and I did not know what the reason was for that, but to tell you now, it was really unusual compared to the previous days, because there were certain incidents before, and I thought that perhaps there would be some kind of incident that day too, but I thought things would pass, that it would not be a major event. About 5.00 we closed the shop. We went to our apartment which was about three kilometres away. As we passed through Kolonija, as we call it, the town, everything seemed rather quiet. There were hardly any people in the streets, and normally we went back to our apartment to get some rest because we were tired. Both my wife and I, we were supposed to have prepared the meat needed for the next day, but we decided we would not do any more work that day but we agreed we would get up very early the next day before I went to the factory and then we would finish that. That is what happened on 15th April. If you have any further questions, please feel free to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The checkpoint goes up to the Vitez road. Was that manned with HVO soldiers that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the checkpoint was about 100 or 150 metres away from my shop and you could see it well from the shop. Members of the HVO were there before, because that is where the main crossroads is for Busovaca, Vjetrenice and also another road to Zenica and they were there before too, but that day the road was closed and there were quite a few vehicles and they would not let them pass. I did not know what was happening there. I found out only later, perhaps after two or three months only what was going on in Zenica then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, could you go back to the photograph that you used before to pick out the Cevapi shop near the Dubravica railway and can you point to the checkpoint you saw HVO soldiers at on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to the crossroads on the upper left-hand portion of exhibit 56?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the road to Vjetrenice, the crossroad of the road leading to Vjetrenice and the road leading to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That evening when you got home, did you watch television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I watched television before quite a lot too, but, to tell you the truth, I did not pay special attention to it that evening, because in Vitez at that time, we were able to watch Bosnian-Herzegovinan television, TV Sarajevo basically, and there was local television, TV Vitez. I do not know, was it run by the HVO or the HVO government, but it was under the control of the Croat authorities anyway, and that evening, I did not watch television, but yes, I did find out, only when I was expelled to Zenica, that there was some kind of TV programme that day, at 5.00 or 6.00, I do not know exactly. Mr. Kostroman spoke, Kordic. They said things could not go on that way, that the Muslims should be disarmed but they were appealing to the Croatian people not to do anything until further orders were issued. I am telling you about this because that is what I had heard, that there was such a television programme, and that is probably the reason why I did not see very many people in the street that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Had you seen programmes with people like Kordic on previously talking about Muslims? Now I am talking about prior to the 15th. Had you seen those types of television programmes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did watch them, but, to tell you the truth, I did not like watching them. Quite often I would turn off the TV set because it was precisely the two of them that were saying quite a few things, warmongering stuff, like: "We cannot live with the Muslims any more; Muslims are to be blamed for everything." Sometimes I would be so upset I would turn off the TV set and I would not watch it any more. I watched some of it but on most occasions I would simply turn off the TV set because I could not listen to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we move to the 16th, Mr. President, if Mr. Dubuisson could put Prosecutor's exhibit 45 on the easel. Mr. Pezer, taking a look at the photograph that is now on the easel and referring it -- for the record, it is Prosecutor's exhibit 45. Could you with the assistance of the pointer point out the location of your house, where you lived on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- perhaps this easel could be turned around a little bit. No, it is okay (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to an apartment building that is just on top of or a block or so on top of the race-track; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am showing the apartment building where I lived; the stadium is a bit lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is fine, sir. If you could just sit down. With the assistance again of the usher and Mr. Dubuisson, if we could turn to exhibit 81, which has been received in evidence, and look at PH337 and PH340. If we could put those on the ELMO, with your assistance, sir? I think it is easier if you take it out of the plastic. If we can take them one at a time, Mr. Usher? Looking at that photograph which is now on the ELMO, PH337 which is part of exhibit 81, is that a photograph of the building where you lived on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Using your pointer on the ELMO, could you point to your apartment on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is, the red balcony (indicating). There is something red on the balcony, rather. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This apartment building is right on the edge of Stari Vitez, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could we then look at the next photograph, PH340? That is a photograph in from Stari Vitez back at your apartment building, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Usher. Mr. Pezer, let us move to 16th April 1993. Do you remember that day? Tell the court about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that on April 15th my wife and I were supposed to prepare meat for the next day. Because we were tired though, we decided to get up somewhat earlier on 16th April, because I was supposed to get to work at the factory, and she was supposed to get to the shop on time, so we decided to get up around 5.00 and perhaps we got up even before 5.00 in the morning. We started preparing the meat straight away so that we could finish that by 6.15 approximately so that I could get to work on time. At about 5.25 or 5.30 or 5.35, within those ten minutes after Ezan, that is a call for prayer, early in the morning at Sabah, I heard strong detonation near my home. I ran to the window immediately to see what was going on, because such situations did occur quite frequently in Vitez over the past few months, and I can say that over 90 per cent of all Muslim shops were blown up, and I think only one or two remained in town, and also this cafe which was near the race-track, the stadium. As I looked through the window, I saw a few soldiers, five or six of them, I cannot remember. They had thrown bombs on this cafe, it was called Trojka and it was owned by Gerina Elvedin. I came back and I told my wife, I said "Gerina's cafe has gone too", and I had no idea that something worse would happen as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you could use the photograph and show the court where you were and where Gerina Elvedin's cafe was that was blown up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, I showed you the other photograph where my balcony was, where my windows were, where my apartment was. My entire apartment was facing Stari Vitez. I could only see Stari Vitez, I could not see the town in any conceivable way. The cafe was on the other side; I will show you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the cafe was on the edge of the stadium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cafe was -- there is a concrete wall around the stadium and the cafe itself was within the stadium and so the outer wall made of concrete was on the other side. Then I told my wife, "There goes Gerina's cafe". I had no idea that something worse was about to take place. I would have to show you what happened afterwards on the map too. They passed on the other side where the garages are, and they moved towards the house of Senad Karalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was Senad Karalic a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was Gerina a Muslim as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continue using the photograph. You said they moved down that street? What did you see next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will show you now where Senad's cafe was. About five or six of them came to the cafe itself. In front of the cafe there was a terrace all in glass. They threw a few bombs there too, I cannot remember how many. Then they moved along the eastern side of that cafe. There were two windows there, one where the bar is and the other where the kitchen is, and they broke the glass on the windows with rifle butts and they threw in bombs. Later one of them walked in with a jerry-can into the cafe, and after a few minutes, I do not know exactly when, the entire cafe was in flames, and it burned down so quickly, it was amazing. I had never seen anything burn down so quickly. It was pretty old and perhaps that is why it burned so fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see one of the soldiers taking a jerry-can in to burn that cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them but I could not recognise them, but it was a soldier. Then, immediately above that cafe, Senad Karalic had a new house, and from the cafe, they moved to that house and a small TAM van was parked in front of the house. They drove it over to this other compound where the garages are, and then they also brought in the luxury car, I cannot remember which luxury car it was, but it was a luxury car. They burned down Senad Karalic's house too, this new house. My wife started crying immediately; she knew Senad and Senad's mother and Senad's wife and Senad's children. We thought they had all burned to death in that house. When they torched the house of Senad Karalic, the next house was the house of Varupa. I do not know the person, I only know him superficially. They were carrying things out of Senad's house and his house. I watched a bit of it and then I would move away from the window, but they were carrying technical goods, probably radios, videos, smaller things they could take along, and then they torched Varupa's house. I know that he is called Varupa but I do not know his name. The next house they torched was Varupa's house. We called him Vare but his name is Mohammed. They went back to torch it three times. In Zenica after a couple of months I saw this man and he told me he was in the house and he tried to extinguish the fire. They kept coming back trying to burn it down but they could not. Part of the house burned down, but that is what he told me; he was in the house and he tried to extinguish the fire. The next house they torched was Latif Barucija's house. All of these houses are in a single row near the garages. In order to burn Latif's house, or rather after burning Latif's house, Hrustic's house was next. They spent some more time there but they came back very quickly, because I saw quite well that one of the HVO soldiers was wounded in the face. I saw blood on his face and probably somebody had put up a fight there. There was a privately-owned home near the apartment building where I lived and soon after that an UNPROFOR vehicle came and parked between Varupa's house and the garages, but the UNPROFOR vehicle stayed there, but they did not pay any attention to this carrier. They kept going back to these torched houses, then they would come back again. At 8.00 or 9.00, I cannot recall exactly the hour, the members of the HVO came into my building, and from the fourth floor, rather from the roof, they opened fire in the direction of Stari Vitez. Then around 2 pm --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before you go to that, sir, before we go to the events at 2 pm, you mentioned that there were a series of houses that you saw being burned, Muslim houses. Could you again go back to the photograph, exhibit 45, and point on the photograph to the houses that you saw being burnt and whether or not those houses are Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the houses that I saw from my window are all Muslim houses, from the crossroads to the next crossroads; I will show you which now (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, you are pointing down a street. All those houses on that street were burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All except one. It was new; probably there was nothing there to burn, so that is why they did not torch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many of those houses were looted of TV sets, videos or other things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I managed to see them taking from Senad's new house and from the old man Varupa's house. From the other Varupa, Mohammed, they took the Lada car and they drove it over. So there were two cars, a truck and some of these electric appliances. I do not know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, you said at 8.00 in the morning the HVO came into the building and began to shoot into Stari Vitez. Where were they shooting from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that about 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning, some HVO soldiers came into your building and started shooting into Stari Vitez. My question for you is: where were they shooting from? Were they shooting from the roof, from the fourth floor, the third floor, where in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were shooting from the fourth floor, and I saw, it was rather difficult to climb to the actual roof of the building, but that morning they were climbing onto the roof. One soldier would stand and another one would climb onto his soldiers and jump up. This building had a flat roof. They were well protected there because I climbed up there myself only a few months before to mount an aerial, so I saw there was a wall behind which they could hide after shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you recognise these soldiers, Mr. Pezer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did two of them. They were young men from Vitez. I think both of them are Krizanac, Nikola and Jako. These are the two I recognised. I knew all the others by sight, but not by name. I could not tell you exactly their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The others you saw by sight, were they from the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were members of the HVO, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said about 2.0 in the afternoon -- you were about to tell us what happened at 2.00 in the afternoon. What happened, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At 2.00, HVO soldiers entered the staircase of the building, and they fired a burst of fire on the ground floor. They ran up the steps and said, "All the Muslims come out." What else could I do but go out, I and my wife. In front of the building, I found about ten or so HVO members; three or four of them had stockings over their heads. I recognised a young man who was in civilian clothes, but he was carrying a rifle. I do not know his name, but I know he is from Mosunj. Knowing me and my wife, he said, "Do not be afraid, there will be no problems, you are just going to the cinema for an interview there and you will be released. Do not panic, do not be afraid." There were seven or eight Muslims on my entrance. We all headed towards the cinema; my wife was with one of the groups. When we reached the cinema they took us into the cellars of the cinema. There were already 20 or 30 people in there, Muslims, of course, who had been arrested, and there were two or three women among them. They begged the HVO members to let them go, they had small children they had left at home. Then I told my wife, since I had a daughter who was 9 in 1993, I told her too, "You go as well. You have a small child; leave me here." They let the women go. Apparently they had been brought in by mistake, but they could now go and I stayed behind with the other Muslims. I already said there were 20 or 30 of us, and they kept bringing in more, and that night, that is 16th April, in the evening in the cellar where the boiler room was of the cinema, there were about 70 or maybe even 80 of us. It was too cramped. People could not lie down; we could hardly sit, never mind lie down. All day they kept bringing in people; this was on the 16th in the afternoon and in the evening. Then they brought in more people but they could not fit into these premises so they took them to the cinema hall itself upstairs. After three or four days, I do not recall exactly how many, they came and told us that some of us would go upstairs to the cinema hall; we would have more room, they said. I did not dare volunteer. I did not think that they intended to move us. I thought maybe they would take us to dig trenches or to do some other labour or even maybe to execute us. Some people did volunteer, thinking it would be better upstairs, so I joined them. I went to the cinema hall, and I stayed there until 30th April. Conditions were much more favourable there than in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, before we move on, let me show you a few photographs. With the assistance of the usher, if we could move to exhibit 33? If we could take three photographs out of there, Mr. Usher, PH197, PH198 and PH203. Looking at the first photograph on the ELMO, which is PH197, Mr. Pezer, do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the cinema; that is the cinema where I was detained for 15 days, only this is a view from the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next photograph, PH198.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also taken from the south. It is the exit from the cinema when the film is over; this is where we went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And PH203?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the cinema.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. With your assistance, if we could put that exhibit back together? Mr. Pezer, if you turn again to the photograph that is on the easel, and you said you were taken from your building to the cinema. Could you trace for the court the path that you took to the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir, you can have a seat. You said, Mr. Pezer, that the people were being brought in all day. Were these all Muslims that were being brought into the cinema, into the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all Muslims. I do not know exactly -- they were all Muslims, yes, but on the third or fourth day, they brought in from the factory Slobodan Princip Seljo, the SPS factory, a few workers who were working that night, the night between the 15th and the 16th, and they were shut up in the factory and later transferred to the cinema and they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are a Muslim yourself, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were in the cinema until the 30th, were there HVO soldiers guarding you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the HVO police, they guarded us, but, to be quite frank, it was possible to escape from that detention, but it was risky, because our families had stayed behind in our homes and apartments, so that no one dared try to escape, because if they were to do that, then their family would not be safe, and there were members of the HVO police there in the cinema.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was this the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were there, were people taken out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were taken out, but by some coincidence I somehow managed to avoid it. We were lying there and somehow I pretended to be asleep, I do not really know how, but anyway I managed to avoid going to dig trenches. There were people who went three or four times. There was one young man, a neighbour of mine where I used to live before -- I do not know how old he was, maybe 18 or 19 -- he got killed while digging trenches and his father was in prison there too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we are going to have a break now until 4.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Bring in the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. Mr. Pezer, we were talking about your time when you were being held in the cinema, and you mentioned trench-digging and you mentioned a young man who was killed while he was trench-digging. How was the selection process made where people were taken out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, we did not know that we were going to dig trenches. HVO policemen would come, the men who were guarding us in the cinema -- they would come with one or two soldiers, I assume they were soldiers from the front, and then he would say, "I need four or five or ten men", and as many as he wanted he would take. By way of example for instance he would say ten, and then, as there were plenty of us, if anyone would volunteer, then he would stand up; if not then he would point a finger and say, "You, you and you come out", and then this soldier would take those men out. Sometimes it was for digging trenches. Then there were some other minor chores like unloading a truck or something like that, but mostly it was digging trenches. As I said, there were people who went four or five times, mostly the people who were closer to the door, and when they walked into the cinema hall, if there were no volunteers, no one had got there voluntarily in the first place, then they would simply point to those people who were close and there was no questioning the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, after you were in the cinema for several days, did you have a conversation with any military policemen concerning an explosion or shelling that he said was going to take place, and if that did happen, can you explain it to the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the cistern that went off in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, a soldier, an HVO soldier, came to the basement. I was in the basement at the time, and we used the toilet which was on the ground floor of the building, and as there were a lot of us we would come and go. We would go to the hall where the toilet was, and then this soldier came and said, "No one should go out because we are expecting some heavy shelling", so that nobody would get hit. Only a little while after that we heard a powerful explosion. We knew immediately that it was not any shelling, because the explosion was very powerful. It was nothing like a grenade or any other device of that kind. Then this same soldier, after this explosion, he came up and said that the Muslims from Stari Vitez had sent a truck full of explosives and this truck went off at the bus station, which was about 200 metres from the cinema. To be quite frank, we doubted the truth of this, because we knew that the Muslims did not have any such thing. That is as much as I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you find out later on exactly what the story was, what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard the next day, I think it was the next day, when my wife came to visit. Who she heard from I do not know, but she told me that this truck-bomb had gone off near the mosque, which is about 150 metres from my building, and all the window panes were shattered on our building and I think one or two doors were also broken from the explosion. It is from her that I heard that this was a truck bomb. When the war ended, I went there and I saw the spot where the explosion occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, was it clear to you at the time that the policeman that told you there was going to be shelling knew that this bomb was going to be set off in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he knew. All of us detainees were suspicious about his statement, because to say that there would be shelling, there were shellings before and they never announced them, so we had our doubts, and immediately; we knew that something was being in the making, and we knew it was not the truth and this was confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, you said previously that you were held in the cinema building until 30th April. Can you tell us about your release, exactly what happened on the 30th and where you went after you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 30th April in the afternoon, we heard from the HVO -- from the policemen that there would be some kind of an exchange, and on that day, Sefer Halilovic the army commander came, Sulejman Kalco, and another one, let me remember -- it does not matter, maybe I will remember later, and on the side of the HVO there was Petkovic, who I did not know, and Mario Cerkez, and apparently they had a meeting -- I just remembered, the third man on behalf of the Armija was Vehbija Karic. They had agreed apparently to carry out an exchange and Sefer Halilovic asked us whether we lived far from the cinema, whether we could reach our homes before nightfall. We said we all lived nearby, however let us see who is going to guarantee our safety when we go home, we said, because there were cases that HVO members would break into apartments and kill people. They find them inside and they simply kill them. Then Mario Cerkez told us that, as far as our safety was concerned, there would be absolutely no problems, the HVO would guarantee our safety. They left, and later two policemen came. One of them, I think he was their commander, Zlatko Nakic, and another military HVO policeman, and they took down our data, where we had worked, whether we belonged to the Armija, when we were born, that sort of thing, and Nakic would write down the date for one set of people and Jurcevic, the policeman, for another set of people. We were suspicious, we were wondering why they were doing these two lists, why one man was not making the records. We learned later, after our release, that the names put down by Jurcevic were released that same day, and those names put down by Nakic, those people stayed behind and I heard from others that they were transferred to the camp in Busovaca. When we were about to be released that evening, they again took us into the office and somebody called Krizanac -- I do not remember his first name; he was working for the Red Cross -- and somebody called Jozic -- I do not remember his first name either, but I know he worked in the SPS factory, and he asked us where we wanted to go, whether we wanted to go home, to Zenica or to Travnik. Where else would I go but home, not just I but all of us, so we all said we were going home so all those whose names were taken down by Jurcevic were released that evening. We went home and the others stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was there some difference between those that were released and the people that were kept and transferred to the prison in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later we worked out what it was about. All the people who had any connections with the BH-Army and the educated people, people who were members of the SDA party, those people were kept on, whereas the others who had no connections with anybody, they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After you were released and you went home -- prior to that, were you given any instructions about whether or not you could leave your apartment? Were you free to travel about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were just given advice. As far as movement is concerned, it was advice that was given to us, not to go anywhere, to stay home. As for my apartment -- not just my apartment, but all the apartments in the building that I lived in, we were ordered on the first day, on 16th April, that the apartments must not be locked. The doors must always remain unlocked, so that when they come to search, they could enter freely. I also forgot to mention that I was a hunter; I had a hunting rifle, of course with a licence. I had an 8577 carbine and a pistol 762. My apartment was searched 88 times. It may sound strange in 15 days, but that is the truth. My wife did not wish to give up my rifle and pistol in spite of the proclamation that all the Muslims had to surrender their weapons whether they were legal or illegal. She surrendered the rifle, I do not remember on what day. It was Zlatko Ruzic who was my neighbour in the same building, and after maybe 13 or 14 days I called up a military policeman of the HVO and told him to go to my apartment with my wife and to take the pistol and to tell them that he had taken the pistol so that they would leave my wife alone, and so he went there with my wife, took the pistol and after that they did not search any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, after you got back home, did the HVO leave you and your family alone, or did the problems continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have problems, only on the first day, but the second day they came just like that. They walked through the apartment, they probably saw that there was nothing to take away because they had already taken away everything on the first day. There was quite a bit of gold, because my wife had quite a bit of it. I have daughters, so they got gold as presents. My video-recorder was taken away, my hunting binoculars, and some other things like that. Then, I think it was on 3rd May in the afternoon, Ibro Gadjun came to my apartment, who was arrested with me and detained in the cinema. He told me that I had to go there to report, that they were looking for me. I said, "Where?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You mentioned "they", the taking of things that were your property and "they" wanted you to report to a location in Vitez. Who are you talking about when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am talking about HVO soldiers. I do not know whether I need to say it every time, but whenever I am saying "they", I am referring to members of the HVO, because they were the ones who held everything under control. Then I asked Gadjun why they wanted me and he said he did not know. I begged him to tell me why I should go there so that I should know what clothes to wear, because it was late in the afternoon. He did not want to tell me, but then I went with him. It is a small house in the Kolonija, where the premises of the local community used to be, and there was a van waiting for us there, and I found seven or eight Muslims there who were already waiting. They themselves did not know why we had come there and where we were being taken to. Then a soldier ordered that we get into the van. He did not want to tell us where we were going, but I saw from the van the direction in which we were being driven, and I told them immediately that we were being taken either to Nadioci or Krisancevo Selo, but they took us to Krisancevo Selo to dig trenches there. We got there, it was quite early before dark fell, they put us up in some weekend houses where the HVO troops rested, then we had a little rest and then they told us to go and dig trenches, but not far away, because it was dangerous, so that we would not be hit by the Armija, so we dug a trench, which was quite safe in the sense that we could not be hit by a gun in that position. When it became dark, they told us we would be taken to the front lines, and they divided us up into twos, into pairs for each dug-out, I and my neighbour Rifet Kajmak dug there, I do not exactly know for how long, but there was a storm in the making. It started to rain and a HVO soldier came and told us, "Let us seek shelter until the storm passes and then we will start digging again afterwards." So we went back to those weekend homes. They were in a kind of valley. The rain continued all night, so that we did not go out again and then in the morning about 8.00 a van came to pick us up and took us back home, or rather to the house in the Kolonija, the small house where the premises of the local community were, and from there we all went to our respective homes. Then in the evening about 10.00 or 10.30, I do not remember exactly, HVO members came to my entrance of the building --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, before we go into that particular incident, can we just clarify some points in the incident where you were taken to dig trenches? Again, using the photograph that is on the easel, Prosecutor's exhibit number 45, could you point to the location on the photograph where you were taken by the HVO out to dig trenches in the van? Could you do that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot on this photograph because I cannot see it there. It is not there. I can show the building that they brought us to, but I cannot show you where we were digging the trenches because it is not shown on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The question I am asking is the building that you were brought to. We will move to the trench location in a moment. What building were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is okay (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to an area near some trees in the centre of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The centre of Vitez, it is pretty dark. There are enormous poplar trees there and probably it was shady when these pictures were taken. This is a very plain house; it is not a big building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you can stay there for a second, with the assistance of the usher, if we could turn to the map which is Prosecutor's exhibit 29, which is over on the wall there, Claudius. Mr. Pezer, do you recognise the areas in that map and the area that you were taken to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to an area on the map. Is that in the area of Tolovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You may have a seat. Thank you. Was that the area that you were taken to dig trenches that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many other men were digging trenches with you that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eight or ten, roughly that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said that, moving ahead, and I cut you off as you were beginning to discuss this, that some HVO soldiers came to your house that evening at about 10.00 or 10.30; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That evening, I think it was the 4th, approximately 4th May. I think it was 4th May, around 10.00 or 10.30. Children were playing in the stairway and among these children was my younger daughter. She ran into our apartment and she told me, "Daddy, here they come." Quite soon after that, they came to my door, and they asked me whether I was Pezer, and I said that I was. They cursed my Balja mother, and they said that I will remember all the things I said and then I asked, "What is it that I have been saying?" One of these soldiers kicked me in the chin, and he asked me how much time I needed to get ready. I understood him to be saying that he was looking for me, and I said, "Me?", and he said, "Not you but you and your family." He said, "I give you fifteen minutes to get ready", and he went further on to the fourth floor and in less than five minutes he came back to the door and he asked whether we were ready. Then I was supposed to take a few things, some clothes that my wife had already prepared, because we were expecting them any day to expel us or simply we were expecting that we would have to flee. I told my wife, "Let us get these suitcases at least to take that along, the clothes of our children." One of these HVO members put out his hand this way (indicates) and he said, "Do not touch anything. Leave everything the way it is and give me the keys to your apartment." I said, "Wait a minute, man", and as soon as I said that he took his rifle and put it under my chin and I went silent. I gave him the keys to the apartment and we went out in front of the building. In front of the building I saw a military policeman from the HVO whom I had known well. I thought that we were on friendly terms, and I asked him, "Dragan, what is this?" He just shrugged his shoulders and said, "I do not know."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Calic, a military policeman. In front of the building a red van was waiting for us. I know that it was owned by somebody from Mosunj, a Croat from Mosunj, I do not know his name. I, my wife and my younger daughter got into the van and then they went to the other building and they brought a woman called Enesa Patkovic from that other building and another man and a woman -- I think they were an elderly married couple; they were refugees from Olovo -- and we got into the van and it drove us to the crossroads of the Zenica road, the road leading to Zenica, and the Vjetrenice road where the HVO checkpoint was, and literally, he threw us out of the van. Again, he cursed our Balja mother and said that we should go to Zenica. It was raining terribly that evening, and we set out in that rain, moving towards Vjetrenice. We did not know where people were until we came up there to Poculica and it was only then we saw that we were on the side that was under BH-Army control. We spent the night at Vjetrenice and on the next day on 5th May we went down to Zenica and I went to the Red Cross to complain. The people at the Red Cross said that it was not possible, and that it was not true. However, I told them everything that had happened to me, just as I am telling you now, and I went to see my wife's brother. We went to his apartment so that I could call Krizanac in Vitez and the other one. I mentioned him a few minutes ago; I cannot remember his name -- Jozic. I wanted to ask them, what was all of that about, what is it for? They told me that what was done to me was not actually so, that they were arresting and even shooting these people who would harass Muslims and they said I should go back to Vitez straight away. Naturally I did not believe that. The next day when I went to the Red Cross, in front of the Red Cross, I saw quite a few people who were expelled from Vitez, on this next evening, on 5th May. I told them about my conversation with Jozic and Krizanac, and they told me that that evening on 5th May about 100 families were expelled from Vitez, the entire buildings of Vitezanka, Banjolucanka, all the Muslims from these buildings were expelled and some others too. At any rate about 100 families were expelled. I saw quite a few of these people and I do not know whether it was 100 people altogether or not, but that is what I heard from them, as I told you, so I did not even think about going back. I simply would not dare to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, could we take the map down and move back to the photograph that was underneath it, please? Mr. Pezer, once again I am asking you to turn your attention back to the photograph. You mentioned that 100 families were expelled from various houses in Zenica on approximately 5th May. Could you go to that photograph and point to the buildings, the three buildings that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is Vitezanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is the top building you are pointing to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Banjolucanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is the next one right below it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Norgorka, these three, these series of three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the record, your Honour, again we are pointing to Prosecutor's exhibit 45. Previously in your testimony you said bags were packed because you were expecting to have to flee. Do you recall saying that just several minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was clear to me that I would have to go, and I gave advice to my wife. I had actually told her beforehand that she should leave with the child and leave me behind, but she did not want to do that. I think that three or four families had already been moved out, and, since these families were moved out, I had suggested to her that she pack these things up, most of them children's clothing, and I told her that if she would have the chance, she should leave, but she did not want to go and I did not think that I would be leaving -- I mean, even when I was released, when he asked me where I would go, I said I would be going home to my apartment. However on 4th May in the evening they forced me out and they would not let me take anything along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were other individuals in your building forced out, both before and after you were forced out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the first one who was forced out of that building, and in mid-May, the other Muslims from that building were expelled too, but all the Muslims from my building were expelled. I was the first to be expelled on 4th May, and after me the others were forced out too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How do you know that they were expelled? Did you see them in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would see each other in Zenica and we would talk to each other. It was only natural we asked each other how we were. I spent some time with these people. Some of them were expelled in a way which was similar to the way in which I was expelled, and -- I do not know how to put this -- others were brought to the line by HVO soldiers and they would call out to others and say: do not shoot; and that is how they would cross the line and go to Zenica and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The personal property you left behind in your apartment, did you ever get any of that property back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you own an automobile at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had an automobile. It was in the garage in that compound consisting of a few garages near the stadium. On 4th May, the automobile was still in the garage, because I saw some children around there. I called out to them, asked them to come to see me underneath my window, and I asked them whether my car was there and they said yes, it was, and I threw 2,000 Croatian dinars out of the window to them and I asked them to close the door of the garage. I simply thought it would be a good thing for me to keep the car, but I was expelled that very evening, so everything was left behind, all my personal property. Also the weekend house I had was burned, the store was destroyed, naturally all my things in the apartment and the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: All gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honours. (Pause). Mr. President, your Honours, we have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. Mr. Hayman or Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have very many questions; we can proceed in two ways. If both Mr. Nobilo and I can question this witness we can proceed immediately. If we have to confer, to prepare one of us to conduct the entire cross-examination, we have to have some period of time to do that. That probably will be perhaps ten, fifteen minutes, not very long, but we need some time, otherwise there is no way for us to combine our cross-examination into one person, one questioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Listen, the Trial Chamber has taken a decision. We cannot go back on a decision that has already been taken. I am looking at my colleagues. In that case, would you like ten minutes to come to an agreement with your co-counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps fifteen because we did not know who the witness would be and we need a little time to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As from now, you know the majority of the witnesses that have been listed by the Prosecution, so you must know how you are going to conduct your Defence, and it will always be one or the other of you. So we will resume at 5.15 for about 20 minutes. We will now have a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Mr. Nobilo or Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Sir, I am interested in the position of your building in view of the frontlines between Stari Vitez and Vitez; or, to put it differently, when you were released from the cinema, and when you came home, where were the positions of the HVO in relation to your building as it faces Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, my building, the entire building was there. There were no trenches or anything there; that is where the line was. There was a privately-owned house near the apartment building and the market, so they were there around the building and the market. The building was in HVO hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we conclude that that building was at the frontline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But when you came, when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, where was the BH-Army in Stari Vitez in relation to your building. Where were they? Where were their strongholds? What did you see when you came back from the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came back from the cinema I was in my apartment for three to four days. I never saw anyone in Stari Vitez, in this Muslim part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That day in the morning, when you were watching the soldiers, you said that one of them had blood on his face, that he was hit in the face. Did you hear some shooting from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some shooting but whether it was from Stari Vitez or from HVO soldiers, I cannot tell, but I can just say that I did not see anyone from Stari Vitez that morning, I only saw members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me: that morning, you recognised two soldiers, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you mentioned their names. Which unit did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the HVO, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But within the HVO, what unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that. I do not know what the setup was like in the HVO because I was not a soldier, until, let me think, 1st June, and I did not know that at all. All of them were HVO to me because they were subordinated to one command, as far as I know about these matters. They had one command which was in the hotel and then they had different commanders or whatever, I do not know how they subdivided this into other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you know that they had a single command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it, I lived there, the command was at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you know that they all obeyed that command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not know. You should ask Mr. Blaskic that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you told us that Vitezovi came to your Cevapi, how did you distinguish between Vitezovi and the other HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally could not distinguish between them, for me they were all HVO members, but I heard that from my wife, that those were Vitezovi, the army of Darko Kraljevic and this same Darko Kraljevic was under the control of Blaskic, as far as I knew about these things. And they also had insignia showing Vitezovi; in addition to HVO they had insignia showing Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you were not involved in army and in politics. How do you know that Darko Kraljevic was under the command of Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Vitez, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is normal that we talk to each other. I heard about that; I lived there with other people in Vitez so we talked a lot about these things and they would say, this is Darko's army or whatever. But they also had insignia of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am asking you: who told you that Darko Kraljevic is under the control of Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: He has given you the answer, Mr. Nobilo. The witness has answered that question. Please continue; go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I tried to get a more precise answer. At the beginning, you said that you thought that there would be conflict between the BH-Army and the HVO, but that problems between the Croat and Muslim people would be worked out, so can you tell me: why did you think that there would be a conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO and what were the problems involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, before 16th April, there were always certain consultations. We would hear this on the radio. Sometimes I would watch the local television but usually I would switch it off because they disseminated these falsehoods and they would say they were meeting here and there and I said I was not interested in the army or whatever. I worked in the factory until the very last day, 15th April. The afternoon of 15th April at 3 pm, I came back from the factory, which is telling proof of the fact that I was not interested in the army and in politics. I am telling you what I heard about. If an incident happened in Zenica and Travnik, this had its reflection in Vitez. After some time the HVO would set up roadblocks. I was an eye-witness. At the bus station they would set up a roadblock and whatever Muslim car came by, they would take them away from them. These were cars owned by civilians. I always thought that civilians would be left alone, and that all these problems that they had between themselves would be worked out between them some day, but this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In addition to what you said here today, do you know anything else about Vitezovi or the army of Darko Kraljevic, as you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did they wear different uniforms from the rest of the HVO at some point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were all sorts of uniforms. There was some kind of HOS, and then there was this HVO. They were camouflage uniforms; they were black uniforms. But the extent to which I saw these people in uniform, over 90 per cent of them had HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On 15th April, in your Cevapi shop in the early evening, there were quite a few people, you said. Were there only Croats and Muslims, or only one or the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were unknown people; I did not know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In addition to the checkpoint towards Zenica, near Vjetrenice, were people free to enter Zenica? Did they say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You spoke of the television which you would turn off. Did you ever see Tihomir Blaskic on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, once I watched him; it was a talk show. Mr. Blaskic was there, Mr. Dzemo Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did Mr. Blaskic say then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was as far back as 1992. There were not any major problems then as far as the army and the HVO is concerned, at least the way I could see things. They had a talk show and viewers were able to put questions, and I for one put a question. I asked Mr. Dzemo Merdan, and he replied. I was wondering what was more important; I did not care about the war and I asked him: what was more important, work assignment or mobilisation; because I was willing to work but I did not want to be mobilised. That was the question I asked, and I saw him on local TV once and that was what I asked. It was a short show, about half a hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was your assessment of Tihomir Blaskic's show then? Was it conciliatory; was it warmongering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, then it was conciliatory. This was 1992 and you probably know what the situation was like in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was your assessment of the situation then in 1992? What is your assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned, an ordinary citizen, there were no major problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, in addition to that appearance of Blaskic on television with Dzemo Merdan, did you hear him on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that it was only later that you heard what happened in Zenica on 15th April 1993. What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That Zenica was blocked, that apparently this commander of the HVO in Zenica was arrested, detained, whatever. I do not know who he was, but I heard about it. My daughter went to school to Zenica and she was supposed to come home during the weekend, but the school was closed that day, and she could not come home because the road was blocked and I do not know what the real reason was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was somebody killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your daughter said that Zenica was blocked. What do you mean "blocked"; by who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could not go from Zenica to Vitez; that is what she told me on the phone. I said then: okay, just stay there. You do not have to come over at the weekend and hopefully things will calm down because there were such situations beforehand too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the date when your daughter said Zenica was blocked and that she could not get out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Either the 14th or 15th, one of those two days, probably the 15th in the evening when we came home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Zenica was blocked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what they say. I do not know whether it was or whether it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you do not know whose soldiers those people who were stealing in Varupa's house were in that street?
