utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I knew who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: HVO members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said you did not know what unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the HVO, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have you made other statements about these things, about these events in Vitez, not today but before; did you make such statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many times and to whom and when and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How many times? I think twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Last year, I think, or the year before last; I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These people, I imagine, from the Tribunal, for investigating war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In what building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the Tzarina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know where the Tzarina is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On both occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that on 10th September 1995 you made a statement; is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that you said then: "I am talking about the people who are torching houses of the two Varupas and who were looting them, that Jako and Niko Krizanac were members of Vitezovi and both of them were dressed in black uniforms." Did you say that on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I did, perhaps I did not, but I do not think that is important at all. The important thing is that that morning, they were in action and I know that they are members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You do not speak English, do you? Do you recognise your signature? Mr. President, could I show the statement that was made earlier by the witness, where he claimed different things, so that he can see his signature? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When you consult with your co-counsel, please switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Sir, did you sign that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know before I read this. It does look like my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I read it out a few minutes ago and I am asking you to state whether you did say this or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I say what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you say that both of the Krizanac men belonged to Vitezovi and wore black uniforms? Is that what you said then or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am telling you again, I am telling you in front of the entire court, for me, all of them are members of the HVO. Who are Vitez and who are somebody else, they had HVO insignia and this same person, Krizanac Jako and Krizanac Niko, they had Vitezovi insignia too, and everybody in Vitez knew they were Kraljevic's army, and Kraljevic again was HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, perhaps you can continue on another subject. The President is going to intervene, because we are departing from the subject. You wish to speak of a statement made previously and that is your right and that is quite legitimate. You have just asked questions which you consider to be useful for the Defence strategy that you have adopted. You had the answer; now we can proceed. Is that agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: However, we did not receive an answer as to whether he said that which I read out on that occasion or not. We have not got that answer yet. So with your permission, we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Wait a minute. For the last time, Mr. Pezer, you are going to put the document on the ELMO. Mr. Pezer is going to look at the statement, confirm that it is your signature, confirm that you made the statement, and the Defence will draw the conclusion it wishes to draw from that. Mr. Pezer, will you look at the statement on the ELMO? You are going to confirm that it is your signature. Is that your signature, Mr. Pezer? Does it look like it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now you are going to take a little time. It is the President who is talking to you: take your time; look at what has been underlined by the Defence, and you are going to tell us whether you can confirm what you said or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness does not speak English, and this is written in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. That is a good remark. Therefore the booth needs to translate into the language of the witness what has been underlined by the Defence, then the witness is going to confirm with yes or no whether he said that and then we can proceed. Can we have this translated? Mr. Nobilo, will you read the part of the text that has been underlined?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I may do so, your Honour. Part of the difficulty here is we have a Serbo-Croatian speaker cross-examining a Serbo-Croatian speaker about a statement that was made in English. That is part of the difficulty of my co-counsel, and I, trying to handle these examinations in the way that we have been ordered to. Could the image be enlarged so that I can read from the video screen, please? If you could focus in on the second full paragraph; thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Among these soldiers that I saw that morning, looting, bombing and incinerating Muslim houses in Stari Vitez, I did not recognise anyone except for Jako and Niko Krizanac, who I know were members of Vitezovi. Both Jako and Niko were wearing black uniform."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, have you understood properly the question that has been put to you? Will you answer it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my statement; however, what is written here should not be written in this way. Probably the person who translated this -- I am trying to say it was not translated properly. This was read out to me. I saw them in the stairway of my building where I lived, when they came from down there, but I did not say they were carrying these things. Most probably the person who was translating then did not translate it properly, but they were in that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you wish to tender this as evidence, despite what the witness has said?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, given that the relevant portion has been read into the record, I do not think it is necessary, unless the court wishes to have the entire statement marked. For our purposes it is not necessary that the entire statement become part of the record. The statement is a hearsay statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the entire statement be put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May we enquire why, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the spirit of totality that the complete statement be put in, not just the paragraph read by the Defence. Let your Honours read the whole statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If we do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, please do not all speak at the same time. Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If statements are admitted wholesale, we will greatly prolong these proceedings because we, the Defence -- or if it is the Defence putting in an entire out-of-court written statement, then the Prosecution -- we will have to cross-examine the witness not only about what they have said in court but about every other statement in the written statement. If that is going to be the practice, we need to know that so that we can cross-examine this witness on these additional out of court statements before the witness leaves the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the spirit of totality, if your Honours want to look at a statement -- the Defence for instance put in a whole newspaper article concerning General Alagic when they only read five lines. The proper method is: if we read a particular extract from a statement, put the whole statement in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the proper method, with all due respect, is to bring the witness to the courtroom, elicit testimony, and subject the witness to cross-examination. If that testimony deviates from a prior statement, each party has the right to seek to impeach that witness. That is the proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is a difference, Mr. Hayman. Please do not lead us into a false logic. What the Prosecutor has said is: when other documents have been submitted, they were submitted in their totality, but it was you who raised the question. You raised the question by extracting this statement and, because it suits you, according to your strategy, to isolate a certain number of sentences, you have asked the questions you wanted; the witness has answered. As from that moment, you are the one who took the initiative to cite this document. Therefore this document will be admitted. The incident is closed and we can now continue with the cross-examination. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will just put another question. Whose evidence is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: To whom are you addressing your question, to the witness or the President?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The Defence proposed as evidence only a citation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So to me it seems to be the evidence of the Defence. You cited it; the Trial Chamber has noted that all that interests you is this particular sentence. The Trial Chamber knows that, but it is no less true that it may need, in the course of its deliberations, to possibly discuss the whole document, saying: yes, the witness answered this; he said something very important. He raised a very important problem in this Trial Chamber, and that is the question of the taking of statements from witnesses which are taken in Serbo-Croatian and they end up in English before the Trial Chamber. So he could not quite find his place in that statement, he wanted to explain his statement and it is therefore quite normal that the whole statement, in the spirit of totality, should be admitted. You wanted only three lines to be cited and to be admitted. It is a Defence exhibit; we the judges know that you extracted only three lines from it. We know that. Therefore, let us continue with the cross-examination. We have only ten minutes left. We are going to work until 6.00. Mr. Hayman, the discussion is over; the question has been settled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We accept that, but we would like to address this at a time convenient for the Chamber. It is very important whether we can use documents to impeach and not have entire documents, hearsay statements then becoming part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I am sorry for being so frank. You have a very Cartesian spirit. It is an honour to the country I belong to, but this is not strictly judiciary logic. Today you invoked a document. It has been entered into the record. Now you say: for the hundreds of witnesses that will be cited, we will do the same. For today, the two judges and the President who is speaking to you find that the witness wanted to explain these three lines. I suppose you wanted to contradict this with another statement he made. He explained it to you; he explained he could not quite identify what he said, and therefore the Trial Chamber has the right to admit this document. On the other hand, the Trial Chamber would make a mistake if it did not take into consideration the objections that you have made. They are in the record. We have nine minutes left. Mr. Nobilo, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The building in which you lived, the side that faces Stari Vitez, was it damaged by bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On April 16th, did you hear any shelling during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some shooting. There were all sorts of things but I cannot really single out shelling and shooting, on the other hand, because there was chaos all over on the 16th, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was the cinema exposed to bullets and to shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During your stay in the cinema, were you physically harassed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the cinema, you said that the military police were there. Was it there before the conflict broke out on 16th April? Did you see the military police when you would pass by there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were several policemen there; I do not know the exact number. Probably they were the security people of that building because before the war in that building of the cinema, on the first floor, the political parties had their offices, the HDZ, the SDS et cetera, and I think that Croatian television was there, and these military policemen were probably the security of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where were they before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The military policemen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were across the street from the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, I mean there in the cinema, that building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you came to this cinema, where were the military policemen then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in the hallway, the very hallway -- as soon as you would walk into the cinema building, they were there, or it was like a reception desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The cinema room, the hall, was it locked when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this side from which we had access to the military policemen, it was not locked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any military policemen with you in the cinema room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were on the other side, as I said, in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did your wife visit you in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would she bring you food or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She would bring me food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you came to Zenica in front of the Red Cross, how many people did you see there from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember how many. I do not know. I was very bitter, it was very difficult for me. I think I did not see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Other people who lived in your building, were some of them exchanged for some other civilians from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the people who lived in the other apartment buildings, those three apartment buildings, the 100 families you mentioned, were they perhaps exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: During trench-digging, were you harassed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was their attitude towards them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps this should be explained. I lived there in that neighbourhood over 20 years, and I knew most of these people, so probably in view of the fact that we had known each other before, they did not do anything, but no, that time when I was there, nobody was harassed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On 3rd May 1993, when you came to dig trenches in Tolovici, were the trenches already dug to a certain point, or were you the first to start digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not completed yet, but digging had already begun before we had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But they were not finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You lived in Vitez for a long time. Did you hear about any municipal agencies that had conducted private exchanges of civilians in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you hear about private municipal agencies that were involved in exchanges of civilians between Zenica and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nobilo. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do not have a statement, so we kindly request a couple of minutes to have a look at the statement so that we could see whether we can use it to cross-examine, because, unexpectedly, we do not have the only copy we had of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you have it, do you not? You produced this statement, Mr. Nobilo. You are talking about the statement of a moment ago? Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, the statement remained there, by the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is a technical problem, all right. Maybe the usher can return your statement to you. Do you have much longer for the cross-examination? You have other questions to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, not very many. Perhaps just a little after we look at the statement once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Switch off your microphone, please. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Judge Riad, do you have any questions to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, and I hope I am pronouncing your name properly, you mentioned cases of detention of civilians in the cinema where you were and then searches in private houses. You spoke of that; you experienced that. Sending people to the front lines to dig trenches. You also spoke about expulsions of a hundred families that were expelled, according to you. Are you capable of telling us, in a general manner, whether all these acts were accomplished by members, official members, of the HVO, or by undisciplined groups in the region, the majority of these acts? Were they disciplined, organised, planned in your view, or were they fortuitous acts taken by people who were under no discipline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, all of this was under control, but see how they did things. For example, from one village, the members of the HVO from Bila for example, they would send them to Kolonija, to the town, and from Kolonija they would send them elsewhere, so they would not know other people, you know what I mean. So my neighbour, for example, who lived with me -- of course I could not say anything bad about my neighbour because he was nice to me, but then I hear from other people that he had gone, for example, to Ahmici, and that he had slaughtered people or massacred people there, but my personal opinion is that all of this was under control. All of this was premeditated, planned, and what they wanted to do, they did; that is to say that nothing was done spontaneously, let us say by a gang or somebody; no, the HVO only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore there was a system, applied in several places? You spoke of your neighbours who went to Ahmici, and they were not from Ahmici, so they were people who according to a planned system accomplished these acts in several different places.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I took Ahmici as an example only. I took that as an example. I did not say that a specific neighbour of mine had gone to Ahmici, but usually they would go to other places to do something so that some day I could not say, "Indeed, that person did such and such a thing." I could not blame him. Had he done something in my building I could have blamed him for that, because that morning of 16th April -- I think there were eight or nine Croat families in my building -- there was not a single man there in the morning. I do not know where they were, but at any rate, every one of them had an assignment of his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you think that this assignment was organised by the HVO, was within the framework of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Also you spoke to us about a very powerful explosion that you heard one day at dawn, after the call for prayer, and you learned the next day that it was a -- you said it was a bomb which exploded close to the mosque. Did I take down well what you said: an explosion close to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are referring to the explosion of the trucks carrying fuel, I do not know. That was about the 20th, I am not sure, the second or third day after the conflict with the HVO. That is when I was detained; that is when that soldier told us not to get out of the cellar because he was expecting heavy shelling and that is when this great explosion took place. It is only later on during the war that I saw how powerful an 82 or 160 grenade was. This was the strongest detonation I had heard ever in my life and I was even in the cellar, and that was the explosion that took place near the mosque, this truck bomb that was sent by the HVO to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Later you could see whether the mosque was damaged or not, and whether there were any people inside in the mosque who were wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mentioned the call to prayer. That was on 16th April in the morning at 5.20 or 5.30. But this was a small explosion, hand grenades that were thrown onto the cafe. What I told you about now, the truck bomb, that was the third or fourth day of the fighting. I do not think that we understood each other correctly. I probably did not understand you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You were speaking about an explosion next to the mosque. Was the mosque empty or were there any people killed inside? That is my question; the date does not interest me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was detained then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Pezer, I gather that you are not a military man yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have lived in Vitez for a long time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In town, from 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You had been accustomed to seeing soldiers in uniform before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You had seen them functioning in a given area before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see soldiers at work in any given area before 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the exception of the barricade along the roads, the roadblocks, the only thing I saw -- just a minute. This was October. The mosque was hit in Stari Vitez by two grenades. I thought that this was shooting from a recoiler's gun, but then later I was told (not interpreted) in October the minaret of the mosque was hit and I heard one shot and the second time I saw it with my own eyes when the mosque was hit. This was October or November, I am not too sure, 1992. Again there was some kind of conflict between the army and HVO and they got this anti-aircraft gun out and hit the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstood that my interest was in the explosion in the mosque. You said you saw soldiers wearing different uniforms, but that they all had the insignia of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you aware of the existence in Vitez of a HVO headquarters then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where were the headquarters of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Vitez hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was the most senior officer at the HVO headquarters in the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know then at that point, probably Blaskic. I do not know who else, out of the locals, I mean the people from Vitez, I knew: Skopljak, Marijan, he was also one of the commanders there, Mario Cerkez. I had a weekend house in the mountain and I had to come to see Skopljak so that I could get a permit to go to my weekend house, and that is how I realised that he was some kind of commander, but I do not know what rank he really had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEN
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have two small questions to address to you. The first is in addition to the question put by Judge Riad, because I did not quite understand your answer, Mr. Pezer. When you spoke of this transfer of men from one village to another village belonging to the HVO apparently, to carry out these acts, my question is: is it your interpretation or is it based on precise facts? Please think it over closely. I will explain further my question. What you said is very serious, because it conveys the idea of a concerted plan, of a policy to send somebody elsewhere to commit atrocities, not in his home and his building but elsewhere, so my question is: is this your interpretation or is it based on interviews, on statements by the military, or is it just an idea that you have, or do you found that idea on very precise facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my idea, but I also want to tell you the following. Kolonija, that is what we call the town where I live too -- all these expulsions were carried out by people who are not from Kolonja. They came from these villages, from the outskirts of Vitez, and that is an obvious example of what was done there as far as Kolonija is concerned. I do not know about other places, that is why I say that I assumed something similar had been done elsewhere too, because as far as Kolonija is concerned and my building, as I said a few minutes ago, that morning on 16th April I did not see any one of my neighbours, the men. On 3rd and 4th May, I would hardly see them, but none of them came to expel me from my apartment. People from Mosunj, members of the HVO, came and expelled by from my apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, you have answered the question. My second question: have you heard anything about Mr. Djidic? Did you work under his orders? What did he do in Vitez and what is your relationship with the Committee for the Protection of Muslims? Did you have any role in that committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in the factory Slobodan Princip Selo. Sefkija Djidic, as far as I know, was one of the bosses up there, and before the conflict where he worked and what he did, that I really did not know, and it says so in my statement that I was not interested in that, that I shied away from such things. I really do not know about this Committee for Protecting Muslims as far as I am concerned, because I worked at such a place -- I had such a job that I was related -- I was closely linked to the factory, and I was pleased that I would not have to take a rifle, a gun and to fight, because people were already going to Visoko and other places, to the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we have concluded. It is rather late, as we can see. Very well, Mr. Pezer, the Trial Chamber wishes to thank you. You are now discharged. We do not need you any more. We will resume the hearing tomorrow at 10.00 am.

procedural_notes.text: (Court adjourned until 10.00 am the following day)
